transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I, um... I hope I'm not wasting your time with this. It's probably just a silly thing I need to get over, but... well, I manage construction sites for a living. And lately, whenever I have to get near a scaffold, or a roof edge, or one of the upper platforms, my head just... it tells me I’m about to go right over. 

It's really embarrassing to even say out loud, because I can look right at it and see the rails are in place, and I know for a fact the setup is completely safe. I mean, I'm usually the one making sure it's safe. But my brain just tells me I'm going to fall anyway. Is that... does that make sense to come see you about?
Do you experience this fear of falling when you're in other high places outside of work, like a balcony or a mountain overlook?

Um, well... I'm actually not entirely sure. I hope that's an okay answer. I just... I guess I don't really find myself on mountains or high balconies very often. 

When I'm off the clock, I mostly just stick to the ground floor, you know? Just keeping things simple, I guess. So I haven't really noticed it happening outside of the job sites. I mean, I probably just steer clear of those kinds of places anyway without really thinking about it too much, just so I don't have to deal with that feeling. Is that... does that help at all with what you're looking for?
Does this fear of falling happen to you when you're thinking about work or a construction site, even if you're not actually there?

No, no, it's really just when I'm actually there, looking down or getting close to the edge. If I'm just sitting at home or in the office looking over blueprints, I'm totally fine. I don't sit around worrying about it or anything like that. I'm a pretty level-headed guy normally, I promise. It's just... in the moment, when I'm up there. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it right.
Is this fear of falling near edges at work causing you any problems with your daily activities or relationships?

Well, I mean... I wouldn't say it's causing huge problems, exactly. I'm still doing my job, mostly. But... well, I guess it has caused a little bit of friction lately. 

I've, um... I've sort of been putting off some of the upper-level walk-throughs. Just delaying them, or sometimes having to skip them if I really can't get myself to go up there. And, well, my crews and the subcontractors, they've kind of started questioning my calls a bit more, which I guess is fair since I'm not up there looking at the work myself. 

And, um, please don't think I'm a bad manager or anything, but... the insurance company for my employer actually pushed for an occupational health review. Because, well, I wasn't completing some of the key safety inspections on the higher levels. I feel terrible about it, I really do. I'm supposed to be the one making sure everyone is safe, and I'm letting them down. Is that... is that the kind of thing you were asking about? I hope I'm not sounding too incompetent.
Do you think you would experience this fear of falling if you were in a similar high place, like a scaffold or roof edge, but not at a work site?

Well, um... I guess I probably would? I'm sorry, I don't mean to be vague. It's just that I haven't really been up on a scaffold or a roof outside of the job in a really long time. 

I mean, I'd like to think I'd be totally fine if I was just, you know, helping a buddy fix his gutters or something. I'd want to be helpful. But if I'm being completely honest... I'd probably get that same awful feeling. I just tend to avoid those situations completely in my personal life, so I haven't really put it to the test. 

Does that make sense? I hope that answers your question okay. I'm really trying to give you the information you need.
Do you think your fear of falling would decrease if you were to change jobs and no longer work on construction sites?

Well, um... I guess maybe? I mean, if I wasn't around edges or high up anymore, I suppose I wouldn't have to deal with that feeling. But... I don't really want to change jobs, you know? I'm good at what I do, mostly, and I really like my team. 

I'd hate to just quit because of this. I want to be able to do my job right, not just run away from it. Do you think there's a way I could just... get over it, without having to leave my career? I'm willing to try whatever you suggest, I promise. I really want to be cooperative here.
Do you think you would still experience this fear of falling if you were on a construction site, but not working?

Well, um... I guess I probably still would? I mean, I'm sorry, I know that's not a very helpful answer. It's just... I think it's the edge itself, you know? Not necessarily whether I'm on the clock or holding a clipboard. 

If I was just standing there, looking down from that height with nothing holding me back... yeah, I'm pretty sure my stomach would still drop and my knees would get all weak. I don't think my brain really knows the difference between working and just visiting when I'm up that high. 

I hope that's the kind of answer you're looking for? I'm trying to be as accurate as I can for you. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture so we can figure this out.
Would you say your fear of falling is only related to your job as a construction site manager, or is it also present in other aspects of your life?

Well, um... I guess I'd have to say it's mostly just the job? I mean, I don't really go out of my way to be on high roofs or cliffs or anything in my free time, so it doesn't come up much. 

I try to keep things pretty grounded on the weekends, you know? Just regular stuff around the house, maybe some yard work. So I don't really notice it then. I hope that makes sense? I'm sorry if I'm not giving you a very clear answer... I just want to make sure I'm explaining it right for you. Does that help at all?
Do you think you would experience this fear of falling if you were in a similar situation, but with no work-related responsibilities or pressures?

Well, um... I think it's kind of like what I mentioned a minute ago? I'm sorry if I'm just repeating myself here, I really want to make sure I'm giving you what you need. 

But yeah, even if I didn't have any deadlines or crew to manage, or any clipboards in my hand... if I'm up near that edge, it's still going to happen. The pressure of the job doesn't really seem to matter, it's just the height itself that gets me. 

I hope I'm understanding your question right? Please let me know if you want me to explain it a different way, I'm happy to try again if that wasn't exactly what you were looking for.
Would you say your fear of falling occurs in any situations where you are not working, but still find yourself in a high place?

Oh, um... gosh, I feel terrible, I feel like I'm just not giving you the right answers since we keep coming back to this. I'm really sorry. 

It's just... like I mentioned a little bit ago, I really don't ever put myself in high places when I'm not on a job site. I don't go hiking near cliffs or visit tall tourist observation decks or anything like that. I try to just keep my weekends pretty normal and safe, you know? So I haven't really tested it out to see what would happen in my personal life. 

I'm so sorry I don't have a better example for you. Is there a specific kind of place you're wondering about? I really want to be helpful here, I just want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need.
Would you say your fear of falling is something that you experience in any situation where you are in a high place, regardless of whether it's related to your job or not?

Oh, um... well, I guess... yes? If I really think about it, I suppose if I were up somewhere high, even if it had nothing to do with work, I'd probably still get that same awful feeling. 

I know I just said I avoid those places, and I do! I really try to. But... well, I guess if I were somehow forced to be up on a tall balcony or something, it wouldn't matter that I'm not at work. The height is what does it. 

I'm sorry, I know I'm kind of talking in circles here. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture. Am I answering this the way you need me to? I really want to be cooperative.
Would your fear of falling occur if you were in a high place with no connection to your job or work responsibilities?

Oh, um... yeah, I think so. I'm sorry, I know we've kind of gone over this a few times now, and I really hope I'm not being difficult or confusing you. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

But yes, if I were up somewhere high, even if it had absolutely nothing to do with my job, I'm pretty sure I would still feel that exact same panic. The work part doesn't really seem to be the issue, it's just... the edge. The height. 

I really hope that makes sense? Please tell me if I need to explain it better, I want to make sure I'm doing this right.
Would your fear of falling from heights completely go away if you were to retire or leave your job as a construction site manager?

Oh, gosh... no, I don't think retiring would fix it. I'm sorry to say that, I know it would be a lot easier if it was just a work stress thing. 

I actually really like my job, and I'd hate for you to think I'm just trying to get out of it or something! But no, even if I quit tomorrow and never set foot on a site again, I'm sure I'd still be terrified of getting too close to a drop-off. The height itself is the problem, not the job. 

I hope it's okay that I'm being so blunt about that? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the clearest answer possible so you can do your job. Am I giving you what you need?
Can you think of any situation outside of work where you've experienced this fear of falling from a height?

Oh, um... I'm really trying to think of a good example for you. I'm sorry, my mind is kind of drawing a blank right now. 

I guess... well, because I know how bad that panic gets, I just naturally stay away from high places when I'm off the clock. Like, I wouldn't ever go hiking near a steep drop or, you know, go to an amusement park with tall rides. So I haven't really put myself in a position to feel it outside of the job in a long time. 

I feel terrible that I can't give you a specific story. Is it okay that I don't have one? I really hope I'm not messing up the assessment by not having a better answer for you. I can try to think harder if you need me to?
Can you recall any instance where you felt this fear of falling when you were in a high place with your family or friends, outside of a work setting?

Oh, gee... I'm so sorry, I'm really trying to dig through my memories here. I feel like I'm letting you down by not having a better answer. 

Honestly, I just... I can't really think of a time like that. Because I know how awful that feeling is, I just make sure I never put myself or my family in that kind of situation. If we go on vacation, I make sure we aren't anywhere near cliffs or tall observation decks or anything like that. I just avoid it completely so I don't ruin the trip for everyone else. 

I'm really sorry I don't have a specific memory to share with you. Does that make sense, though? That I just avoid it? I hope that's an okay answer... I really want to be helpful here.
Would you say your fear of falling from heights is something that you experience equally in both work and personal settings, or is it more prominent in one over the other?

Well, gosh... I guess because I avoid high places so completely in my personal life, I really only ever feel that awful panic when I'm at work. Not because the job makes it worse, but just because... well, I can't avoid it there, you know? I have to be up on the scaffolding or checking the upper floors. So it definitely feels like it's more prominent at work, just by default. 

I hope that makes sense? I'm sorry if I'm talking in circles or making this complicated. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. Did I explain that okay for your notes?
Would you experience this fear of falling if you were in a situation where you were in a high place, but it had no connection to construction or your job as a manager?

Oh, um... yes, absolutely. I'm sorry, I should have been clearer about that before. 

If I were up high somewhere totally unrelated to work—like, say, if I went to a tall monument on a family trip or something—I would definitely still feel that same terrible panic. The fear isn't about the job or the construction site itself at all. It's strictly about the height and that feeling that I might fall. 

I just... I'm really careful to never let myself get into those situations when I'm off the clock, so I don't have to put my family through seeing me like that. I really hope I'm explaining this right. Does that help clarify things for you? I'm sorry if I made it sound like it was just a work thing earlier.

Would you consider your fear of falling to be something that is only related to your work as a construction site manager, or is it a more general fear of heights that you experience regardless of the context?

Oh, um... well, it's definitely a general fear. I'm so sorry, I think I'm repeating myself a bit, aren't I? I don't mean to be confusing. 

Like I was trying to say, it's really just the height itself that terrifies me, no matter where I am or what I'm doing. It's just that work is the only place I can't hide from it. If I had an office job, I'm sure I'd feel the exact same way if I had to look out a high window or stand on a balcony. It's not the construction site, it's just... the drop. 

I really hope I'm answering this the way you need me to. I know I'm probably not the easiest person to interview since I don't have a lot of examples outside of work. Am I giving you what you need for your assessment? I can try to explain it differently if that would be better.
Do you think your fear of falling would occur if you were in a very high place, like a mountain or a tall building, with no edge or drop-off in front of you, but still very far above the ground?

Oh, um... you mean if there's no edge? Like if I was just inside a tall building or on a big, wide mountaintop? 

Gosh, I'm actually not totally sure. I guess I've never really thought about it that way, because I just try to avoid anything high up altogether. I suppose if I couldn't see the drop or get near an edge... maybe it wouldn't be as bad? But honestly, just knowing I'm that high up usually makes my chest tight. I'm sorry, I wish I had a better answer for you. I just haven't really tested it out, you know? I hope it's okay that I don't know for sure. Does that still help with your evaluation, or should I try to think of a specific time that happened?
Would your fear of falling occur if you were in a high place but couldn't see the ground below?

Oh, um... if I couldn't see the ground? Like, if the windows were frosted or I was in the middle of a big room up high? 

I... I don't know for sure. I'm sorry, I feel like I'm not being very helpful with these questions about being up high but not near an edge. I guess if I couldn't actually see the ground down below, it might not be quite as terrifying? But just knowing I'm up there... it still makes me really anxious. I try so hard just to keep my feet on the ground whenever I can, so I don't really have a good example for you. 

I'm really sorry I don't have a clear "yes" or "no" for that one. Am I messing up the interview by not knowing? I can try to imagine it harder if you need me to.
